bib.title: AutoLab: Can Frontier Models Solve Long-Horizon Auto Research and Engineering Tasks?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AutoLab: Can Frontier Models Solve Long-Horizon Auto Research and Engineering Tasks?" First author Zhangchen Xu (equal contribution with Zichen Chen, the corresponding author). Affiliations: University of Washington, Stanford, UCSB, UCSD, Notre Dame, Princeton, NUS, Waterloo, MIT, NVIDIA, Bake AI, Google, MIT-IBM Watson, and an independent researcher. arXiv 2606.05080v1 [cs.AI], 3 Jun 2026. No venue is stated, so it is a preprint.

COVERAGE: 28 of 28 pages, 89,511 chars. I read the abstract through the conclusion in full, plus Appendix C and the Table 7 tail. I only skimmed the references and the Appendix A/B task descriptions and per-task tables.

CORE CLAIM: On 36 long-horizon optimization tasks, the paper says persistence predicts success better than one-shot quality. Persistence means repeatedly benchmarking, editing and using feedback. Many strong models either quit early or burn the whole budget without submitting.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. **Main ranking.** claude-opus-4.6 scores Avg@3 0.68, Best@3 0.76, Dominance 0.93. The runner-up, gemini-3.1-pro, scores Avg@3 0.50.
   - Setup: 11 flagship models, 36 tasks, 3 rollouts per (model, task), terminus-2 agent in the Harbor harness, wall-clock budgets of 2 to 12 hours. The whole evaluation used 2,544 wall-clock hours and 8.60 billion tokens (Table 1, p.7).
   - gpt-5.4 scores Avg@3 0.36 and grok-4-20 scores 0.35.
2. **Persistence evidence is correlational and shown only in plots.** The paper reports a "clear positive correlation" between score and both agent steps and agent runtime (Fig. 5, p.8).
   - opus-4.6 had a median of 57 steps against 12 for gemini-3.1-pro (p.7).
   - The text gives no correlation coefficient and no direct test of "initial attempt quality" against persistence.
3. **Zero-score rollouts.** The authors manually inspected 302 zero-score rollouts across the 11 models (Fig. 6, p.9). The four failure modes are Timeout/Context Exhaustion, Capability Gap, Instruction Violation and Others.
   - Timeout-dominated: deepseek-v4-pro, hunyuan-3-preview, qwen-3.6-plus.
   - Early submitters: gpt-5.4 and grok-4-20.
   - deepseek-v4-pro on the CUDA subset: 9 of 12 trials submit fewer than 10 actions before the timeout.
4. **Harness changes the score.** Scores were compared across three harnesses on 25 CPU tasks, with 4 models and Avg@3 (Fig. 7, p.11).
   - kimi-k2.6 moves from 0.21 on pi-mono to 0.64 on mini-swe-agent* (Δ0.43).
   - mini-swe-agent* is the paper's modified harness whose system prompt says not to submit at first pass.
   - deepseek-v4-flash scores 0.54 on mini-swe-agent* at about $0.07 per trial.
   - kimi-k2.6 costs $0.40 per trial on pi-mono and $2.05 on mini-swe-agent*.
   - Rankings are non-transitive. gpt-5.4 scores 0.50 on pi-mono, 0.40 on terminus-2 and 0.37 on mini-swe-agent*.
5. **Run-to-run variance.** Stability is in Appendix C.2 (Table 8, p.28). opus-4.6 has mean per-task standard deviation 0.099. For the four models with CV ≥ 0.40, the mean range across trials is 0.28–0.34. The gap between Best@3 and Avg@3 grows with σ (Pearson r = 0.84).
   - Table 8 lists opus Avg@3 as 0.77 and Best@3 as 0.85. Table 1 gives 0.68 and 0.76 for the same models. I could not reconcile the two.

QUOTES
- p.1 (abstract): "the dominant predictor of success is not the quality of an agent's initial attempt, but its persistence in repeatedly benchmarking, editing, and incorporating empirical feedback."
- p.8–9: "This early stopping directly limits their optimization potential and largely explains why several proprietary frontier models rank low in the benchmark."
- p.11: "harness-induced variance can be comparable to model-induced variance."

LIMITS
- The persistence claim rests on cross-model correlation plots and a trajectory case study (flash_attention, p.7). The text reports no coefficient and no controlled test.
- Opus's lead is confounded by model, step count and token use. The paper does not intervene on persistence in the main harness. The only partial test is the persistence-prompting mini-swe-agent*, run on 4 models and 25 CPU tasks.
- Only 3 rollouts per cell, and per-task variance is large.
- The authors say the benchmark covers "measurable auto-research" (executable system and ML engineering tasks), not scientific discovery in general.
- Models are February–April 2026 vintage and have dated. It uses a single default harness, terminus-2, and no small open-weight models (under 200B parameters). Failure labelling was manual, with no inter-rater check reported.

BUILDS ON
- Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026): the Harbor harness, the terminus-2 agent and the task-audit criteria.
- AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) and Karpathy's autoresearch (2026): the closed-loop optimization idea. The paper criticises both for bespoke harnesses.
- KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025), MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2024), RE-Bench (Wijk et al., 2024), PostTrainBench, Frontier-Eng and others.
- SWE-agent / mini-swe-agent (Yang et al., 2024).

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION
In 06-evaluating-agents.md, "Efficiency metrics" (line 292) and its "Convergence in practice" subsection (line 309) fit best, because the finding is about steps and runtime against score and about early quitting. "Non-determinism: run every task k times" (line 253) is a good secondary home for the Avg@3 vs Best@3 and σ result. "Environment hygiene" (line 391) fits the harness-variance result. The target note has no existing AutoLab citation.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
- Fig. 5 (p.8–9): score against agent steps, runtime and cost.
- Fig. 4 (p.8): flash_attention runtime against wall-clock time per model, which shows persistence directly.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Figure and table text extracted messily, and some Fig. 1 numbers were scrambled. I used only the Table 1 numbers.
- Table 1 and Table 8 disagree for opus (see headline number 5).
